newsitem.title: UK: POLL - Experts see morality debate helping UK Labour.
newsitem.headline: POLL - Experts see morality debate helping UK Labour.

text.p: The main opposition Labour party, tipped to win a clear majority in Britain's coming general election, has gained a short-term fillip from a morality debate raging in the country, a Reuters poll on Wednesday showed.

The latest survey of political experts showed on average that Labour was expected to win a majority of 39 seats in the lower House of Commons, compared with a majority of 37 tipped in the Reuters September poll.

The experts judged the current debate on political sleaze and public morality would help Labour on balance but said it would probably peter out as a big issue as the election, which must be held by May 22, draws near. Nine out of the 20 psephologists and independent analysts surveyed expect a brief upsurge in Labour support from the morality debate. The remaining 11 did not believe it would help either Labour or the ruling Conservative party.

Predictions on the overall result in the survey ranged from a Labour majority of 125 to a Conservative majority of nine in the House of Commons, which will have 659 seats after the election compared with 651 now. Peter Kellner, an independent political analyst, believes allegations of sleaze and hypocrisy levelled against the Conservatives, who have been in power since 1979, mean that any gains from the debate will be for Labour. "But my feeling is, it's a short-term thing and won't have a lasting effect. The small, temporary benefit is for Labour," Kellner said.

Following the murder of London headmaster Philip Lawrence, stabbbed to death at the gates of his school, his widow Frances has launched a moral crusade that is currently galvanising Britain's main political parties.
The survey, carried out between October 25 and 30, showed that on average Labour is expected to win 347 seats and the Conservatives 260 seats.
From the September survey, John Benyon, professor of politics at Leicester University has changed his views significantly. His forecast for the Labour majority has more than doubled to 49 from 23.
"The Conservatives have been in power since 1979.....it's difficult to blame anyone else," Benyon said.

David Carlton, a lecturer in international studies at the University of Warwick, was the only expert to expect a Conservative victory, with a majority of nine seats. Its current overall majority is just two. At the other extreme, John Curtice, senior lecturer of politics at Strathclyde University in Glasgow, expects a 125- seat majority for Labour.
He said: "If the government is going to recover, it needs to demonstrate competence and retake control of the agenda."
Asked what the major issues in voters' minds were now, most contributors cited unemployment and the government's perceived competence -- or lack of it.

By the time of the election, expected by a majority of the panel to be held in May, worries about tax and the single currency that the European Union plans to launch in 1999 could also emerge, they said.

Signing up for the single currency would lead to loss of control over the exchange rate and restrict Britain's room for monetary manoeuvre, with the risk that unemployment could rise to European levels, said Sydney Elliot, senior lecturer in politics at Queen's University in Belfast.
Most of the opinion polls carried out this year have given Labour over 50 percent of the vote and the Conservatives under 30 percent.

However, survey participants expect the gap to be narrower, around six percent, when voters actually cast their ballots, with Labour expected to draw around 42 percent support and the Conservatives 37 percent.
